title: Visual hierarchy — Image Wiki
text:
Visual hierarchy
  The order in which your eye visits the parts of an image — decided by the image, not by you.

  
    Termvisual hierarchy
    Also calledfocal point, dominance, emphasis, eye path, center of interest
    Not the same asbalance, rule of thirds, subject matter
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat pulls, roughly in order of strengthWhat changes when you change itWhat goes wrongCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Open the next image you have to judge and answer one question before you think about anything else: where did your eye land first? Not where it should have landed. Where it went, in the moment before you started reasoning.
Then notice something uncomfortable. You did not decide that. You can decide to stay somewhere, but the first landing is not yours. The picture made it happen.
That first landing, and the second and third after it, is what people mean by visual hierarchy. The thing that wins is the dominant element; the runners-up are focal points; everything else is background. Three levels is what most people can actually tell apart, which is why designers stop at three (SRC-031).
Why it happens
You see sharply in a very small patch. The fovea, the high-resolution centre of the retina, covers about two degrees of your visual field — roughly a thumbnail held at arm's length. Everything outside that is blurry and colour-poor, and gets worse fast toward the edges.
So your eye jumps. Three or four times a second it repoints that tiny sharp patch somewhere new, and the periphery picks the target. Peripheral vision cannot read text or recognise a face, but it is very good at noticing where a patch of the field differs from the patch next to it.
That is the whole mechanism, and it forces a correction most people need:
The eye is pulled by contrast against the local surroundings, not by brightness in absolute terms.


Dark subject in a light field: Hiroshige, Kanbara, evening snow
Light subject in a dark field: Joseph Wright of Derby, The Alchemist


Utagawa Hiroshige, Kanbara, Evening Snow, from The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, c. 1833–35 (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston). Joseph Wright of Derby, The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, 1771 (Derby Museum and Art Gallery). Both public domain.
Opposite polarity, identical result. In the Hiroshige the whole field is white snow and the darkest things in it are three small travellers — and that is where you land, on figures a few percent of the frame. In the Wright the field is a near-black vault and the brightest thing is the glowing flask at the lower right — and that is where you land, before you have noticed there are four people in the room.
Now check what does not pull in the Hiroshige: the grey sky across the top is darker than the snow and much bigger than the travellers, and it attracts nothing. A wide area of one even tone has no internal difference to offer. The pull comes from a local mismatch, not from a tone being dark, or bright, or large.


If you have been taught "the eye goes to the brightest area", drop it. A dark shape among fifty other dark shapes is invisible; the same shape alone in a pale field is a shout.
What pulls, roughly in order of strength

Value contrast against the immediate surroundings. The most reliable pull by a wide margin, and the one that survives squinting.
Faces, and within a face, the eyes. Brejon calls it recognition emphasis: human shapes take attention off objects almost regardless of size (SRC-098).
Sharpness against blur. A crisp region inside a soft one reads as the thing worth looking at — the reason shallow focus works as a pointing device.
Isolation. An object that groups with nothing, because nothing is near it or resembles it, becomes a focal point through sheer loneliness (SRC-098). See Gestalt grouping.
Convergence. Perspective lines, a road, a table edge, a gaze. Where lines meet, the eye goes, even if nothing is there.
Colour difference. Weaker than value, and it dies when the image is viewed small or converted to grey.
Size. Real but overrated. A big low-contrast thing gets noticed less than a small high-contrast one (SRC-033, SRC-030).




Gordon Parks, American Gothic, Washington, D.C. (Ella Watson), August 1942. Farm Security Administration / Office of War Information, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Size and brightness both lose here, which is why this frame is a good test of the list above. The broom is the largest object in the picture and one of the palest; the flag is larger still. Your eye went to her face — a few per cent of the area, darker than everything around it, and sitting near the middle of the frame.
Two things prop it up. Her face is the sharpest region in the frame: the flag's stars are visibly soft, so the lens is pointing at her and nothing else. And her glasses draw two small high-contrast rings around the eyes, which is where recognition emphasis is strongest of all.


What changes when you change it



Change
Effect on the eye path




Darken the background behind the subject
Subject jumps forward; hierarchy sharpens


Raise saturation everywhere
Hierarchy flattens — nothing is different any more


Blur the background
Subject wins, cheaply and reliably


Add a second face
You now have two dominant elements, whether you wanted them or not


Crop out a bright corner
Often a bigger improvement than anything you do to the subject



Notice the pattern: hierarchy is a competition, so you fix it either by strengthening the winner or by weakening the field. Weakening the field is usually easier and almost always looks less forced.
What goes wrong
Two equally strong attractors. The eye goes A, then B, then back to A, and never settles. Co-dominance is allowed, but the two then need a relationship — a gaze, a gesture, a line between them — or you have a tug of war (SRC-031). A different complaint from an unsteady frame; see Balance.


One focal point: a single man on a store porch
Several competing: six men and a wall of signs on another store porch


Russell Lee, Man on porch of general store near Jeanerette, Louisiana, October 1938 (cropped by us to match the other panel's shape). Dorothea Lange, Country store on dirt road, Gordonton, North Carolina, July 1939. Both Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain.
The same subject twice — people on the porch of a rural general store, loud advertising behind them — with opposite hierarchies.
On the left there is one place to look and you found it immediately. Note how little the signs manage: "666 COLDS FEVER" is black lettering on white, the highest local contrast on that wall, and it still loses to a face in a shadowed hat. His only real competitor is the white sleeve of the man cropped at the left edge, which is why that edge keeps nagging.
On the right, say your landings out loud: the standing man in the white shirt, the Texaco star, the "Chesterfields Satisfy" panel, the Coca-Cola sign, then the row of seated men, none of whom outranks his neighbours. Every element is fine on its own. What is missing is a ranking, and without one the eye keeps circling. That is the mechanism behind "it looks busy" — not too much stuff, but no order to visit it in.


The background out-pulls the subject. A blown-out patch of sky between two branches, a white plug socket beside a head, a stranger's red jacket at the frame edge. The accident wins because contrast does not care what the picture is about. This is the most common reason an image reads as amateur, and a crop fixes it about half the time.



Dorothea Lange, Toward Los Angeles, California, March 1937. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Answer honestly: what did you look at first? Almost certainly the billboard, not the two men. The board is the whitest rectangle in a grey photograph, it has a hard black edge all round it, and it carries text — three of the strongest pulls stacked in one place. The men are dark clothes against a mid-grey road, a much smaller local difference, and they are facing away.
Lange wanted that competition; the caption is the joke. But the mechanism is the one that ruins ordinary photographs, and the dominant element here is not the subject. Cover the right third with your hand and the men become the picture immediately.


Everything emphasised. Bold, bright, large, saturated, sharp, all at once. Emphasis is relative: if all of it shouts, none of it is heard (SRC-031).



Marion Post Wolcott, Center of town, Woodstock, Vermont, "snowy night", 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Two attractors ranked properly. The lamp wins outright: it is the only small patch of blazing white in a dark field, while everything else bright here is either large and even (the snowbanks) or small and dim (the shop windows at the right).
Then watch the second mechanism arrive. The trodden footpath, both snowbanks and the line of parked cars all run toward the lamp post, so convergence points where contrast already pulled, and the two agree. Cover the lamp with a fingertip: the frame goes aimless at once, though nothing else has changed.


Common mistakes

"The subject is the biggest thing, so it is the focal point." Size loses to contrast, to faces and to sharpness. Check where your eye actually goes rather than which object occupies the most area.
"The eye goes to the brightest part." Only if bright is the local difference. In a high-key image the eye goes to the darkest part.
"There is no hierarchy in this image." There is always a hierarchy — the question is whether it is the one anybody intended. A photo with no designed focal point still has a first landing, usually somewhere embarrassing.
"Hierarchy is about the composition, not the light." Value contrast is the strongest attractor there is, and value contrast is made by lighting. See Value structure.


Reading the hierarchy of an image

Where did your eye land first? Answer before analysing — you only get one attempt per image.
Where did it go second, and third? Say it out loud as a path.
Squint until detail disappears. What still stands out is the real hierarchy.
Is the first landing the subject? If not, name what beat it, and ask whether that thing is meant to be there.
Does the eye settle anywhere, or ping-pong between two things and leak out of a corner?



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              How to look at an image
              A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Balance
              Why one frame feels steady on its feet and another feels like it is tipping over, even though nothing in a picture weighs anything.
            
          
        
          
            
              Gestalt grouping
              The automatic machinery that turns a field of pixels into objects and groups — and the reason accidental alignments in a photograph look deliberate.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
